A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite reformatting and added appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original NEURON simulations, fitted energy-noise relationships, and numerical analyses of tuning-curve adaptation and homeostasis, including in its appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulation results and adds Gabor and correlated-noise analyses, plus likelihood comparisons using previously published biological data.

M1.justification: The central homeostasis and energy-constrained optimization remains intact. Appendix H.4 replaces the eighth-degree noise polynomial with a 17-parameter fourth-degree polynomial times an exponential, with nonnegative fitting parameters. Appendix J changes the b2 fit from quartic to quadratic. Appendix N also introduces a correlated-noise adaptation of the optimization.

E1.justification: The mouse visual-cortex data and natural-scene orientation prior are retained. Appendix N extends evaluated noise conditions to differential correlations, including differing correlation strengths across control and food-restricted states. The Gabor extension changes the model configuration within the retained orientation task.

E2.justification: The reference methods remain Ganguli and Simoncelli (2010) and Wang et al. (2016a), corresponding to references [5] and [30] in v1. Tables 2 and 5–7 and Figure 4 retain them; the new likelihood analysis reuses these comparators.

E3.justification: v2 adds likelihood-based evaluation using responses summarized from 29 control and 32 food-restricted cells, Gabor-base evaluations, and a numerical correlated-noise protocol. Appendix N uses energy settings 1 and 0.76, correlation strengths up to 1000, and penalty weights 10, 100, and 1000. The original biophysical simulation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's objective, prior, and activity-level analyses, v2 tests homeostasis with Gabor base shapes in Appendix L.3 and robustness to differential correlations in Appendix N. Penalty-weight sensitivity and constraint-error analyses additionally check whether the new broadening results arise from numerical artifacts.

E5.justification: Both versions report 10,000 simulation trials per cell condition. v2 introduces no new seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates for the authors' results. The added likelihood scores measure fit; neuronal noise dispersion remains a modeled quantity.

E6.justification: Appendix J replaces fitted coefficients and adaptation results, including changing eta0 from order 10^9 to near 1. New results include Gabor firing-rate deviations from -0.45% to -0.31%, likelihoods of -155 for Ganguli and Simoncelli, -107 for Wang, -85 for the proposed model, and -47 with optimized dispersion. Appendix N reports approximately 4% additional correlation-related broadening versus 38% metabolic broadening in its new setting. Figure 9's values are unchanged; its accompanying 2% bound is corrected to 0.2%.

T1.justification: The core propositions and analytical derivations in Appendices A–E are retained. Appendix M adds likelihood derivations and a parameter-calibration formulation; Appendix N introduces correlation-adjusted Fisher information and a penalized optimization formulation. These extend the mathematical treatment without replacing the central closed-form results.

C1.justification: The central claims about ATP-based constraints, generalization of earlier codes, and homeostatic flattening are retained. Section 3.2 adds an explicit claim that the solutions remain robust to differential correlations, including changes across metabolic states, extending their stated applicability beyond v1's independent-noise treatment.

C2.justification: v2 adds biological mechanism explanations in Section 2 and Appendix F. Appendix M substantially qualifies empirical fit because the two conditions contain different cells, and identifies unvalidated calibration stability and local minima. Appendix L.3 distinguishes Gabor homeostasis from still-unverified optimality. Appendix J replaces the earlier high-activity reliability warning with deviations concentrated at lower activity after refitting.

D1.justification: v2 documents the new noise-fitting formula and constraints, and specifies the correlated-noise optimizer's step size of 0.001, 3000 iterations, and penalty settings. Existing NEURON parameters, hardware, runtime information, and the reference to supplementary simulation code are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of firing-rate energy proxies in Gutierrez and Deneve, Koren and Panzeri, Koren et al., and Tavoni, while retaining the original positioning. Moreno-Bote et al. (2014) is added to motivate differential correlations. These are localized extensions of related work.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing exposition remain. v2 moves motivation from the discussion into the introduction, expands Appendix F into a simulation overview, adds explanatory summaries, and consistently clarifies 'firing probability' as 'spike count.' These are targeted revisions rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 10–14 for Gabor responses, correlated-noise sensitivity, and penalty diagnostics. Existing noise-fit and adaptation plots are revised, including Figures 3 and 6–8. The ICLR format changes the title block, headers, table styling, and figure placement, while retained Figure 9 redisplays the same results.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central flattening prediction by testing non-Gaussian base shapes, differential correlations, and numerical artifacts that v1 left unexamined. The revised Appendix J calibration also resolves the inconsistency between v1's enormous reported dispersion offset and its near-unit dispersion curves. Appendix M adds quantitative fit comparisons with explicit biological-data limitations. Gabor optimality and calibration stability remain incompletely validated, but the gains in assumption testing, numerical consistency, and transparency are substantial.
